math_questions.question: Devon took 7 quizzes and earned a mean score of 87 points. If the mean score for the first 5 quizzes was 84 points, how many points did Devon score on the 7th quiz?

solution.exhibit_text: Sum of first 5 quizzes: 5 \times 84 = 420. Sum needed for all 7: 7 \times 87 = 609. The 7th quiz score is 609 - 420 = 189.

base_question.question: Annette took 6 quizzes and earned a mean score of 85 points. If the mean score for the first 5 quizzes was 82 points, how many points did Annette score on the 6th quiz?

solution.exhibit_text: Recall that \(\text{Average}=\dfrac{\text{Sum of Values}}{\text{Number of Values}}\). Let \(x\) represent the sum of the first five quizzes. You are told that Annette's mean score on the first five quizzes was 82, so \(82=\dfrac{x}{5}\) and \(x=410\); Annette scores 410 total points on her first 5 quizzes. You also know that the mean score of six quizzes is 85. Let \(y\) represent the score on the 6th quiz. Therefore, \(85=\dfrac{410+y}{6}\). Multiply both sides by 6 to get \(510=410+y\) and \(y=100\).

solution.exhibit_text: P(first white) = 7/12. After removing one white, P(second white) = 6/11. Multiply: 7/12 x 6/11 = 7/22.

base_question.question: A utility drawer contains \(4\) red rubber bands and \(6\) white rubber bands. If two rubber bands are picked at random without putting the first one back, what is the probability that both rubber bands are white?

solution.exhibit_text:
Recall that \(\text{Probability}=\dfrac{\text{Number of Desired Outcomes}}{\text{Number of Total Outcomes}}\). First, find the probability that the first rubber band is white. There are \(6\) white rubber bands and \(4+6=10\) total rubber bands, so the probability is \(\dfrac{6}{10}=\dfrac{3}{5}\). Now find the probability that the second rubber band is white. After the first white rubber band is picked, there are only \(9\) rubber bands left, and only \(5\) of them are white. Therefore, the probability that the second rubber band picked is white is \(\dfrac{5}{9}\). To find the probability of both rubber bands being white, multiply their respective probabilities:

\[\dfrac{3}{5}\times\dfrac{5}{9}=\dfrac{3}{9}=\dfrac{1}{3}\]

math_questions.question: A flat circular metal washer has an outer radius of 11 millimeters. The circular hole in the center of the washer has a circumference of \(8\pi\) millimeters. What is the area of the metal face of the washer?

options.A: 15\(\pi\) sq mm
options.B: 44\(\pi\) sq mm
options.C: 60\(\pi\) sq mm
options.D: 105\(\pi\) sq mm

solution.exhibit_text: Outer disc area = \(\pi(11^2)=121\pi\). Hole circumference 8\(\pi\) = 2\(\pi\)r, so r=4. Hole area = \(\pi(4^2)=16\pi\). Metal area = 121\(\pi\)-16\(\pi\)=105\(\pi\) sq mm.

base_question.question: A flat circular metal washer has an outer radius of 9 millimeters. The circular hole in the center of the washer has a circumference of \(6\pi\) millimeters. What is the area of the metal face of the washer?

options.A: \(12\pi\) sq mm
options.B: \(36\pi\) sq mm
options.C: \(45\pi\) sq mm
options.D: \(72\pi\) sq mm

solution.exhibit_text: The area of the metal face of the washer is the area of the circular metal disc minus the area of the circular hole. The formula for the area of a circle is \(\pi r^2\). Since the outer radius is 9 mm, the area of the disc is \(\pi(9^2)=81\pi\) sq mm. To calculate the area of the circular hole, find the radius from the given circumference. The formula for circumference is \(2\pi r\). Since the circumference of the circular hole is \(6\pi\) mm, \(2\pi r=6\pi\) and \(r=3\) mm. Thus, the area of the circular hole is \(\pi(3^2)\) sq mm. Putting everything together, the area of the metal face of the washer is \(81\pi-9\pi=72\pi\) sq mm.

math_questions.question: The population of City Y was 600,000 in 2016 and 450,000 in 2018. If the percent decrease from the 2018 population to the 2020 population is the same as the percent decrease from 2016 to 2018, what should the 2020 population be?

base_question.question: Based on the graph above, if the percent decrease from the \(2018\) population to the \(2020\) population of City \(X\) is the same as the percent decrease from the \(2016\) population to the \(2018\) population, what should the \(2020\) population in City \(X\) be?

solution.exhibit_text:
For this question, you have to know not only how to read graphs, but also how to find a percent decrease. The bar above \(2016\) reaches to \(5\) on the graph, and the graph is in units of \(100{,}000\), so the population in \(2016\) was \(500{,}000\). The population in \(2018\) was \(400{,}000\). To find the percent decrease in population, divide the amount of decrease by the original amount and then multiply by \(100\%\).

\[\left(\dfrac{500{,}000-400{,}000}{500{,}000}\right)\times100\%=\dfrac{100{,}000}{500{,}000}\times100\%\]
\[=\dfrac{1}{5}\times100\%=20\%\]

If the percent decrease in population from \(2018\) to \(2020\) is the same as the percent decrease from \(2016\) to \(2018\), then from \(2018\) to \(2020\), the population should also decrease by \(20\%\). \(20\%\) of the \(2018\) population is \(20\%\) of \(400{,}000\), or \(80{,}000\), so the \(2020\) population should be \(400{,}000-80{,}000=320{,}000\).

math_questions.question: If \(x=5(2-y)(3^2-2)\), what is the value of \(y\) in terms of \(x\)?

base_question.question: If \(x=4(3-y)(2^2-1)\), what is the value of \(y\) in terms of \(x\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
Finding the value of one variable *in terms of* another variable just means to solve for the first variable, \(y\). You won't get a numerical answer, but rather an answer that still has the other variable in it, \(x\). Start by simplifying the right-hand side of the equation. Then, solve for \(y\). You may have to manipulate the result to make it match one of the answer choices.

\[x=4(3-y)(2^2-1)\]
\[x=(12-4y)(4-1)\]
\[x=(12-4y)(3)\]
\[x=36-12y\]
\[x-36=-12y\]
\[\dfrac{x-36}{-12}=y\]
\[\dfrac{x}{-12}-\dfrac{36}{-12}=y\]
\[\dfrac{-x}{12}+3=y\]
\[3-\dfrac{x}{12}=y\]

math_questions.question: Points are plotted on a coordinate plane: J(1,5), K(3,4), L(2,2), M(5,2), N(2,6), P(3,9), R(6,3). Which line segment, if extended, represents a proportional relationship?

options.B: \(\overleftrightarrow{KL}\)
options.C: \(\overleftrightarrow{LR}\)
options.D: \(\overleftrightarrow{NP}\)

solution.exhibit_text: A proportional line must pass through the origin (0,0) -- meaning y = kx for a constant k. base_question.question:
Which straight line is the graph of a proportional relationship?

(Coordinate plane with points labeled: M(1,8), P(3,6), V(2,2), Q(6,2), T(1,4), R(2,8), S(8,0).)

options.A: \(\overleftrightarrow{MS}\)
options.B: \(\overleftrightarrow{VP}\)
options.C: \(\overleftrightarrow{VQ}\)
options.D: \(\overleftrightarrow{TR}\)

solution.exhibit_text:
(D) The graph of any proportional line must intersect the origin, \((0, 0)\).

The **only** line on the coordinate plane that contains \((0, 0)\) is \(\overleftrightarrow{TR}\).

Both point \(T(1, 4)\) and point \(R(2, 8)\) have a \(y\)-value that is \(4\) times the \(x\)-value, and every point on the line fits the proportional equation \(y = 4x\).

When \(x = 0\), \(y = 4(0)\). So the line contains the origin, \((0, 0)\).

math_questions.question: The hash marks on a number line are evenly spaced, with point M at \(-\dfrac{1}{8}\) and point T at \(\dfrac{3}{4}\), with 4 equal sections between them. Point R is 2 sections away from M (toward T). What is the coordinate of point R?

base_question.question: The hash marks on the number line above are evenly spaced. What is the coordinate of point \(R\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) There are \(5\) sections between \(M\) and \(T\). To find the length of one of these sections, find the distance between \(M\) and \(T\) and divide by \(5\):

\[\left(\dfrac{5}{8} - \left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\right) \div \dfrac{5}{1} =\]
\[\left(\dfrac{5}{8} + \dfrac{2}{8}\right) \div \dfrac{5}{1} =\]
\[\dfrac{7}{8} \div \dfrac{5}{1} = \dfrac{7}{8} \times \dfrac{1}{5} = \dfrac{7}{40}\]

\(R\) is \(3\) sections away from \(M\), so add:

\[-\dfrac{1}{4} + 3\left(\dfrac{7}{40}\right) = -\dfrac{10}{40} + \dfrac{21}{40} = \dfrac{11}{40}\]

\(R\) is located at \(\dfrac{11}{40}\).

options.B: B
options.C: C

solution.exhibit_text:
Separate the compound inequality into two pieces: \(-(a+5)<\dfrac{b}{-2}\) and \(\dfrac{b}{-2}\le-3-a\). Then plug in 4 for \(b\) and solve each inequality for \(a\). Be careful to flip the sign when multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative.

First piece: \(-(a+5)<\dfrac{4}{-2}\)
\[-a-5<-2\]
\[-a<3\]
\[a>-3\]

Second piece: \(\dfrac{4}{-2}\le-3-a\)
\[-2\le-3-a\]
\[a\le-1\]

Combining both pieces gives \(-3<a\le-1\), so choose the number line with an open circle at \(-3\), a closed circle at \(-1\), and shading in between, (B).

math_questions.question: Six numbered cards are placed on two tables: Table A holds cards numbered 21 and 24. Table B holds cards numbered 31, 33, 35, and 38. Elena randomly picks one card from Table A and places it on Table B. Then, Omar picks a card from Table B at random. What is the probability that both cards picked will be a card with an even number on it?

solution.exhibit_text: P(Elena picks the even card, 24) = 1/2. If she does, Table B now has 2 even cards (24, 38) out of 5, so P(Omar picks even) = 2/5. Multiply: 1/2 x 2/5 = 1/5.

base_question.question: Six numbered cards are placed on two tables as shown in the figure above. Ryana randomly picks one card from Table A and places it on Table B. Then, Vera picks a card from Table B at random. What is the probability that both cards picked will be a card with an even number on it?

solution.exhibit_text:
To calculate the probability of an event happening, use the following formula:

\[\text{Probability}=\dfrac{\text{Number of Desired Outcomes}}{\text{Number of Total Outcomes}}\]

Since there are two independent events in this question, calculate the probability of each one individually and then multiply their probabilities together.

The probability that Ryana will pick an even-numbered card from Table A is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).

Keep in mind that if Ryana picks an even-numbered card, there will be 1 more even card on table B for Vera to choose from. Thus, there are now 2 desired outcomes and 5 possible outcomes: \(\dfrac{2}{5}\).

Finally, multiply these probabilities together: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{5}=\dfrac{2}{10}=\dfrac{1}{5}\).

math_questions.question: Which of the following decimals is equivalent to \(2\dfrac{1}{3} + 1\dfrac{5}{9}\)?

options.A: \(3.\overline{6}\)
options.B: \(3.\overline{8}\)
options.C: \(4.\overline{1}\)
options.D: \(4.\overline{8}\)

solution.exhibit_text: Convert to a common denominator of 9: 2 1/3 = 7/3 = 21/9, and 1 5/9 = 14/9. Add: 21/9 + 14/9 = 35/9 = 3 8/9 = 3.888... = 3.\overline{8}.

base_question.question: Which of the following decimals is equivalent to \(1\dfrac{2}{3} + 2\dfrac{4}{9}\)?

options.A: \(3.\overline{1}\)
options.B: \(3.\overline{6}\)
options.C: \(4.\overline{1}\)
options.D: \(4.\overline{9}\)

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) First, add the mixed numbers. Then, convert the fraction \(\dfrac{1}{9}\) to a decimal.

\[1\dfrac{2}{3} + 2\dfrac{4}{9}\]
\[1\dfrac{6}{9} + 2\dfrac{4}{9}\]
\[3 + \dfrac{10}{9}\]
\[3 + 1\dfrac{1}{9}\]
\[4\dfrac{1}{9} = 4.111\ldots = 4.\overline{1}\]

math_questions.question: What is the value of \(z\) in \(\dfrac{p}{6} + \dfrac{q - p}{3} = \dfrac{z}{6}\)?

options.B: q
options.C: p
options.D: 2q - p

solution.exhibit_text: Multiply every term by 6: p + 2(q-p) = z. Distribute: p+2q-2p=z, so z = 2q-p.

base_question.question: What is the value of \(z\) in \(\dfrac{x}{10} + \dfrac{y - x}{5} = \dfrac{z}{10}\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
(D) First, multiply both sides of the equation by \(10\) to eliminate the fractions. In other words, multiply each term by \(10\).

\[\dfrac{x}{10} + \dfrac{y - x}{5} = \dfrac{z}{10}\]
\[10\left(\dfrac{x}{10} + \dfrac{y - x}{5}\right) = 10\left(\dfrac{z}{10}\right)\]
\[\dfrac{10x}{10} + \dfrac{10(y - x)}{5} = \dfrac{10z}{10}\]
\[x + 2(y - x) = z\]

Then, distribute and combine like terms to find the value for \(z\).

\[x + 2(y - x) = z\]
\[x + 2y - 2x = z\]
\[2y - x = z\]

math_questions.question: A debate club has 9 members: 6 are ninth graders, and 3 are eighth graders. The club needs to choose a President, a Secretary, and a Treasurer. If no member can hold more than one office, how many different ways can the positions be filled, given that the President must be a ninth grader?

solution.exhibit_text: The President must be a ninth grader, so there are 6 choices for President. That leaves 8 students for Secretary, then 7 for Treasurer. Multiply: 6 x 8 x 7 = 336.

base_question.question: A school's robotics club has 8 members: 5 are eighth graders, and 3 are seventh graders. The club needs to choose a President, a Vice President, and a Treasurer. If no member can hold more than one office, how many different ways can the positions be filled, given that the President must be an eighth grader?

solution.exhibit_text:
You are told that the President must be an eighth grader. There are 5 eighth graders, so there are 5 choices for the President.

There are no constraints on the remaining positions. Since one eighth grader has already been chosen, there are now a total of \(8-1=7\) students left. There are thus 7 choices for the Vice President. Once this position is assigned, there are only 6 choices for the Treasurer. Putting everything together gives \(5\times7\times6=210\) total ways the positions can be filled.

How much money will Talia have left or still owe if she uses the money her aunt gave her to pay back the money she borrowed?

options.A: Talia will still owe \(\$3.00\).
options.B: Talia will still owe \(\$4.00\).
options.C: Talia will have \(\$3.00\) left.
options.D: Talia will have \(\$4.00\) left.

solution.exhibit_text: Total borrowed = 9.25+13.0+6.75 = 29.00. Gift minus borrowed = 32.0-29.00 = 3.00. Since this is positive, Talia has \(\$3.00\) left over.

base_question.question: Maxie borrowed $\(7.75\) from her mother, $\(11.00\) from her father, and $\(4.50\) from her brother to purchase a video game. Her grandmother gave her $\(25.00\) as a gift. How much money will Maxie have left or still owe if she uses the money her grandmother gave her to pay back the money she borrowed?

options.A: Maxie will still owe $\(2.25\).
options.B: Maxie will still owe $\(1.75\).
options.C: Maxie will have $\(1.75\) left.
options.D: Maxie will have $\(2.25\) left.

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) First, determine the total amount Maxie borrowed, in dollars:

\[7.75 + 11.00 + 4.50 = 23.25\]

Then use subtraction to determine the difference between the amount her grandmother gave her and the amount she borrowed:

\[25.00 - 23.25 = 1.75\]

The difference is positive, which means that Maxie will still have $\(1.75\) left from the amount her grandmother gave her.

base_question.question: Which graph represents the solution to \(|x-2| \le 3\)?

options.A: A
options.B: B
options.C: C
options.D: D

solution.exhibit_text:
Absolute value makes the output positive by ignoring the sign of the number. This means that the input can be either positive or negative. Thus, \(|x-2| \le 3\) implies both \(x-2 \le 3\) and \(-(x-2) \le 3\).

Rewriting the second inequality gives \(x-2 \ge -3\). Remember that the inequality sign flips when dividing or multiplying by a negative. Solve the first inequality for \(x\):

\[x-2 \le 3\]
\[x \le 3+2\]
\[x \le 5\]

Solve the second inequality for \(x\):

\[x-2 \ge -3\]
\[x \ge -3+2\]
\[x \ge -1\]

Thus, \(-1 \le x \le 5\). Since the symbol is \(\le\) (inclusive), use solid (closed) circles at \(-1\) and \(5\). The variable \(x\) is between \(-1\) and \(5\), so the line segment connecting these two points should be shaded.

Alternatively, use Backsolving. Since 0 is a solution for (C) and (D) but not in (A) and (B), let \(x=0\). When \(x\) is 0, \(|-2|\le 3\) is true. Thus, eliminate (A) and (B). Now, let \(x=4\). When \(x\) is 4, \(|4-2|\le 3\) is true. Thus, (D) is correct.

math_questions.question: Suppose that $p$, $q$, $r$, and $s$ are non-zero integers. Under which set of conditions would the expression \(p^3 q |r| s^2\) always be negative?

options.A: $p$ is negative and $q$ is positive.
options.B: $r$ is negative and $s$ is positive.
options.C: $r$ is positive and $s$ is negative.
options.D: $p$ and $q$ are positive, and $r$ and $s$ are negative.

solution.exhibit_text: |r| and s^2 are always positive regardless of sign. For the whole product to be negative, p^3 and q must have opposite signs. Only (A) guarantees that: p negative makes p^3 negative, and q positive, so they differ in sign.

base_question.question: Suppose that \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), and \(d\) are non-zero integers. Under which set of conditions would the expression \(a^3b|c|d^2\) always be negative?

options.A: \(a\) is negative and \(b\) is positive.
options.B: \(c\) is negative and \(d\) is positive.
options.C: \(c\) is positive and \(d\) is negative.
options.D: \(a\) and \(b\) are positive, and \(c\) and \(d\) are negative.

solution.exhibit_text: The expression \(a^3b|c|d^2\) is the product of four terms: \(a^3\), \(b\), \(|c|\), and \(d^2\). Two of the terms, \(|c|\) (the absolute value of \(c\)) and \(d^2\), will always be positive. The other two terms, \(a^3\) and \(b\), can be either positive or negative. In order for the product of all four terms to be negative, either \(a^3\) is negative and \(b\) is positive, or \(a^3\) is positive and \(b\) is negative. In other words, \(a^3\) and \(b\) must have different signs. Of the choices, only (A) has a set of conditions that would cause \(a^3\) (a negative number cubed is a negative number) and \(b\) to have different signs.

math_questions.question: Which situation involves quantities that combine to equal zero?

options.A: spending $8 on lunch and then earning $8 doing chores
options.B: buying a notebook for $8 and then buying a pen for $8
options.C: getting on an escalator at the ground floor, rising 2 floors, and then rising 2 more floors
options.D: starting on a diving platform 10 feet above the pool, diving down 10 feet, and then swimming down 10 feet more

solution.exhibit_text: Look for two values with the same size but opposite sign. Spending $8 is -8, earning $8 is +8, and -8 + 8 = 0.

base_question.question: Which situation involves quantities that combine to equal zero?

options.A: receiving $\(5\) as a gift and then giving $\(5\) to a friend
options.B: buying a book for $\(10\) and then buying lunch for $\(10\)
options.C: getting on an elevator at the ground floor, rising \(3\) floors, and then rising \(3\) more floors
options.D: starting in a cave \(20\) feet below the ground, climbing up \(20\) feet, and then climbing up \(20\) feet more

solution.exhibit_text:
(A) When looking for a situation where quantities combine to make zero, find two values with the same absolute value where one value is positive and one value is negative.

In the situation in option A, receiving a gift of $\(5\) is represented by \(+5\), and giving a friend $\(5\) is represented by \(-5\). These values combine to equal zero because \(+5 - 5 = 0\).

math_questions.question: In rectangle WXYZ, the length of WZ is 8 units and triangle TYZ has an area of 64 square units. Point T is the midpoint of WX. What is the length of WT?

solution.exhibit_text: The area of triangle TYZ relates to WZ (the base) and WT (half of WX, the height): area = WZ x WT, so WT = area / WZ = 64/8 = 8.

math_questions.question: Which of the following numbers has a factor that includes the smallest factor (other than 1) of 85?

solution.exhibit_text: 85 = 5 x 17, both prime; the smallest factor other than 1 is 5. Numbers ending in 0 or 5 are divisible by 5. Only 25 fits.

base_question.question: Which of the following numbers has a factor that includes the smallest factor (other than \(1\)) of \(95\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
Numbers that end with \(0\) or \(5\) are divisible by \(5\). The number \(95\) is a good candidate for prime factorization: \(95=19\times5\). These are both prime numbers, the smallest being \(5\).

(B) \(21\) factors to the prime numbers \(3\) and \(7\).

math_questions.question: A closed rectangular storage bin measures 18 cm long, 12 cm wide, and 8 cm high. What is the total surface area, in square centimeters, of the closed storage bin?

base_question.question: The figure above shows a closed rectangular storage bin. What is the total surface area, in square centimeters, of the closed storage bin?

solution.exhibit_text:
The total surface area is the sum of the areas of all six faces (top, bottom, front, back, left side, right side). The area of the top (and bottom) is length \(\times\) width, the area of the front (and back) is length \(\times\) height, and the area of the left side (and right side) is width \(\times\) height. Thus, the formula for the total surface area is \(2(lw+lh+wh)\). Plug in \(20\) cm for \(l\), \(15\) cm for \(w\), and \(10\) cm for \(h\):

\[SA=2[(20)(15)+(20)(10)+(15)(10)]\]
\[=2(300+200+150)\]
\[=2(650)\]
\[=1{,}300\text{ cm}^2\]

math_questions.question: Last week, Jordan rode the bus to school on 4 of the 6 mornings and rode the bus home on 3 of the 6 afternoons. Based on last week's events, what is the probability that Jordan will ride the bus in the morning and the afternoon next Monday?

solution.exhibit_text: P(morning) = 4/6 = 2/3. P(afternoon) = 3/6 = 1/2. Multiply (independent events): 2/3 x 1/2 = 1/3.

base_question.question: Last week, Emily rode the bus to school on \(3\) of the \(5\) mornings and rode the bus home on \(4\) of the \(5\) afternoons. Based on last week's events, what is the probability that Emily will ride the bus in the morning and the afternoon next Monday?

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) Using the joint probability formula, find the product of the two independent events. The probability that Emily will ride the bus to school on any given morning is \(\dfrac{3}{5}\). The probability that Emily will ride the bus to school on any given afternoon is \(\dfrac{4}{5}\).

Therefore, the probability that Emily will ride the bus in the morning and the afternoon is \(\dfrac{3}{5} \times \dfrac{4}{5} = \dfrac{12}{25}\).

math_questions.question: Each month, Noor incurs fixed operating expenses of \(\$1800\) at her pottery studio. It costs her \(\$45\) to produce a specific ceramic vase, and she sells each vase for \(\$110\). What is Noor's profit if she produces and sells 50 vases in 1 month?

solution.exhibit_text: Profit per vase = 110-45 = 65. For 50 vases: 50 x 65 = 3250. Subtract fixed costs: 3250 - 1800 = 1450.

base_question.question: Each month, Maya incurs fixed operating expenses of \(\$2{,}400\) at her boutique. It costs her \(\$60\) to produce a specific designer dress, and she sells each dress for \(\$140\). What is Maya's profit if she produces and sells \(40\) dresses in \(1\) month?

solution.exhibit_text:
Profit is sales minus expenses. Maya sells each dress for \(\$140\), and each dress costs her \(\$60\) to produce. Therefore, her profit is \(\$140-\$60=\$80\) on each dress. She produces \(40\) dresses in \(1\) month, so her profit on her dresses is \(40(\$80)=\$3{,}200\). Her fixed expenses each month are \(\$2{,}400\). Therefore, her total profit is

\[\$3{,}200-\$2{,}400=\$800\]

math_questions.question: Priya speed walks 4 kilometers in \(\dfrac{4}{5}\) hour. At that rate, how many meters does she speed walk per minute?

solution.exhibit_text: 4/5 hour = 48 minutes. 4 km = 4000 meters. 4000 \div 48 = 83 meters per minute.

paragraphs.text: Grace Murray Hopper was 37 when she enlisted in the Navy in 1944 in response to the outbreak of the Second World War. Her extensive career spanned the transition from the very first electromechanical computers to the birth of modern high-level programming. While many of her contemporaries focused on the hardware—the vacuum tubes and switches—Hopper focused on the human side of computing. An advanced mathematician herself, she believed that computers should be accessible to people who weren't mathematicians.
The Harvard Mark I: Where It All Began

After joining the U.S. Naval Reserve, Hopper was assigned to the Bureau of Ships Computation Project at Harvard University. There, she became the third person to program the Harvard Mark I, a 50-foot-long behemoth of switches and relays.

Working on the Mark I was grueling. Programs were fed into the machine via punched paper tape. There was no operating system; you had to understand the physical architecture of the machine to make it do anything. It was during this time that Hopper famously helped popularize the term "debugging." When a moth flew into a relay of the Mark II and caused a system failure, she taped the insect into the logbook, noting that they were "debugging" the machine.

However, her most significant contribution at Harvard wasn't just fixing errors; it was her realization that mathematical code was too difficult for most people to master. She began thinking about ways to make programming more intuitive.
The Invention of the Compiler

In 1949, Hopper joined the Eckert-Mauchly Computer Corporation (which later became part of Remington Rand) to work on the UNIVAC I, the first large-scale commercial computer. It was here that she did her most revolutionary work: the invention of the compiler. The compiler translates code words that humans can understand into the electrical pulses that control the computer's machinery. Before Hopper's breakthrough, if you wanted a computer to perform a task, you had to physically flip switches or re-wire parts of the computer. Because of her work, we can simply change a word in a text file, called the source code, and let the compiler do the hard work of translating it for the hardware.

Hopper believed that a computer could be programmed to translate human words into computer commands. In 1952, she developed the A-0 System, the first compiler. It allowed a programmer to use words instead of mathematical codes. Her work was ignored at the time because, as she said, "I had a running compiler and nobody would touch it because, they told me, computers could only do arithmetic; they could not write programs." Engineers argued that a machine could never write code as efficiently as a human. They believed automated code would be slow and wasteful of the very limited memory available in early computers. Hopper also faced the prejudice of early programmers who were mathematicians. They felt that if you couldn't handle the complex arithmetic of machine code, you shouldn't be allowed to touch a computer at all.

Hopper realized she couldn't win the argument with theory; she had to win it with utility. She knew that processing all the data needed to run a business, such as payroll, billing, and taxes, was the future of computers. Businesses didn't want to hire a team of highly trained experts to run a payroll. They wanted their accountants to be able to talk to a machine that could do it.

In 1956, she released FLOW-MATIC, the first programming language to use English-word commands such as GET, COMPARE, and MOVE. To prove it worked, she didn't just show the code—she showed the results. She demonstrated that a program written in English-like commands could run on the UNIVAC and produce accurate business reports. Her experiment proved that even if the compiled code was slightly less efficient than hand-written code, the time saved in writing the program made up for that. A person could write a FLOW-MATIC program in a day that would take a machine-code expert a week.
The Birth of COBOL

Hopper's innovation changed the way computers were programmed. By 1959, every computer manufacturer had their own specific compiler and language. The computing world was a mess of different languages. A program written for one machine wouldn't work on another. If a company bought a new machine, it had to throw away all its old programs and start over. Hopper championed the idea of machine-independent languages.

In 1959, she served as a technical consultant to the committee that created COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language). COBOL was heavily based on her FLOW-MATIC philosophy. Its goal was to allow businesses to process data using a language that managers could actually read.

COBOL became the most widely used business language in the world. Even today, decades later, a massive percentage of the world's financial transactions are still processed by COBOL code. Hopper's insistence on a standardized, English-based language is why modern writing instructions rather than wiring a circuit board.
Legacy

Grace Hopper retired from the Navy multiple times, only to be called back because her expertise was indispensable. When she finally retired for the last time at age 79, she was a Rear Admiral and the oldest active-duty officer in the U.S. Navy.

Every time you write a line of code in Python, Java, or C++, you are using concepts that Grace Hopper fought to prove were possible. By breaking down the barriers between human language and machine code, Hopper ensured that the power of computing would belong to everyone, not just a select group of experts.
A Comparison of FLOW-MATIC and Python Computer Instructions
(In this scenario, the computer is to check the number of an item in stock and print a message if the number is too low.)
Philosophy — FLOW-MATIC: "Tell the computer in English sentences." | Python: "Clean, readable, and minimal."
The Code — FLOW-MATIC: (1) COMPARE ON-HAND-STOCK TO MINIMUM-STOCK ; IF GREATER GO TO OPERATION 10 ; IF LESS GO TO OPERATION 5 . | Python: if on_hand < minimum:
The Action — FLOW-MATIC: (5) MOVE "REORDER NOW" TO PRINTER ; WRITE-ITEM PRINTER ; GO TO OPERATION 10 . | Python: print("Reorder now")
Logic Flow — FLOW-MATIC: Relied on GO TO jumps (rigid). | Python: Uses indentation and blocks (structured).

questions.question: How do the details in paragraphs 5 and 6 help convey a central idea of the passage?

options.A: They document how Hopper's background as an advanced mathematician allowed her to master complex machine code.
options.B: They provide a justification for why the A-0 System was slower and more memory-intensive than manual machine coding.
options.C: They suggest that the development of modern programming was driven by the needs of the U.S. Naval Reserve.
options.D: They emphasize how Hopper's innovations were designed to prioritize human access to computers over computer efficiency.

solution.exhibit_text:
Category: Global
Getting to the Answer: Review the Main Idea. The passage has a strong positive tone and describes several of Hopper's important discoveries that changed computing. Now review paragraphs 5 and 6: they describe Hopper's compiler as her most important ("revolutionary") work, despite the resistance to its acceptance. Match this prediction to (D), the correct answer. These paragraphs show how Hopper's compiler "prioritized human access" by using "code words that humans can understand" instead of prioritizing "computer efficiency," as other engineers thought computers couldn't write code "efficiently."
(A) is a Misused Detail. The text explicitly states she was an "advanced mathematician" (paragraph 1), but the point of these paragraphs is that Hopper wanted to move away from math-heavy code to make computers easier for others. (B) is also a Misused Detail. The paragraph mentions that the A-0 System was slower, but this is not a central idea of the passage. (C) is Out of Scope. Although paragraph 12 mentions that her "expertise was indispensable" to the Navy, paragraphs 5 and 6 do not address this idea.

questions.question: What does Hopper's comment in paragraph 6 reveal about the challenges she faced?

options.A: Because others viewed computers as only mathematical tools, Hopper faced obstacles in her career.
options.B: The limited memory of the computers of Hopper's time meant that creating a compiler was very difficult.
options.C: Despite Hopper's advanced degrees in mathematics, other mathematicians believed she lacked sufficient training to develop a compiler.
options.D: The early computer companies preferred to keep programming difficult in order to maintain control over their products.

solution.exhibit_text:
Category: Detail
Getting to the Answer: Locate Hopper's comment in paragraph 6 and read around it to understand the context. The third sentence tells you that "Her work was ignored," and the last part of her quotation says "because, they told me, computers could only do arithmetic; they could not write programs." Match this idea to (A), the correct answer.
(B) is a Misused Detail. Although the memory of the computers of the time was very limited, Hopper had a "running compiler," so she had overcome that obstacle and is not referencing it in the quote. (C) and (D) are Out of Scope. The passage never mentions Hopper being criticized for lacking training (C) or the intentions of computer companies (D).

questions.question:
Read these sentences from paragraph 6.

Engineers argued that a machine could never write code as efficiently as a human. They believed automated code would be slow and wasteful of the very limited memory available in early computers.

The words "slow" and "wasteful" in the sentences convey the idea that

options.A: the compiler was viewed as a threat to the precision and craftsmanship required for machine-level programming.
options.B: Hopper's critics misunderstood how the A-0 System translated mathematical codes into electrical pulses.
options.C: the use of English-word commands was seen as a distraction from the mathematical rigor necessary to maintain computers.
options.D: many computer engineers prioritized the conservation of resources over the ease of the programmer.

solution.exhibit_text:
Category: Function
Getting to the Answer: Start by establishing the context for the words in the question. Your Roadmap should indicate that paragraph 6 discusses the resistance to Hopper's compiler. In the context of early computing, "slow" refers to processing time and "wasteful" refers to the use of the "very limited memory." These are both concerns about the resources of the computer, reflecting the engineers' argument that Hopper's use of more user-friendly coding would make computers less efficient. Match this prediction to (D), the correct answer. All the other choices are Out of Scope. The passage does not describe the compiler as a "threat" (A) or mention any "misunderstandings" (B) or "distractions" from the math (C).

questions.question: Which statement describes how the author's use of a problem-and-solution structure in paragraphs 9 and 10 contributes to the development of ideas in the passage?

options.A: Highlighting the competitive nature of the 1950s technology boom explains why early computer manufacturers were reluctant to collaborate.
options.B: Establishing the necessity for a standardized language like COBOL emphasizes the inefficiency of having multiple programming languages.
options.C: Detailing the technical limitations of 1950s hardware shows why Hopper's FLOW-MATIC was eventually replaced.
options.D: Suggesting that Hopper's primary motivation was to increase corporate profits illustrates the financial burden on businesses.

solution.exhibit_text:
Category: Function
Getting to the Answer: Use your Roadmap to help you identify the problem-and-solution. In paragraph 9, the problem was that "every computer manufacturer had their own specific compiler and language," so that "a program written for one machine wouldn't work on another." This created a "mess" in which companies had to "throw away" existing programs when buying a new computer. The paragraph transitions to the solution by stating that Hopper "championed the idea of machine-independent languages," which leads directly into the discussion of the COBOL language in paragraph 10. Match this summary to (B), the correct answer.
(A) is incorrect because it is Out of Scope. Competition among computer manufacturers is not discussed. (C) is Opposite. The passage uses the limitations of computers to illustrate why it was important to apply Hopper's FLOW-MATIC philosophy to COBOL. (D) is a Distortion. Hopper's motivation was to improve access to computers, not to increase profits.

questions.question: With which statement would the author most likely agree?

options.A: The initial resistance to the compiler was a necessary phase that ultimately made COBOL the most efficient language for global commerce.
options.B: The complexity of modern coding languages such as Python and Java makes them fundamentally different from the English-based philosophy of FLOW-MATIC.
options.C: Hopper's most enduring legacy is her successful challenge to the belief that computing should be reserved for mathematical experts.
options.D: Although English-based computer languages are easier to use, the loss of the "physical architecture" knowledge has made modern programmers less capable than their predecessors.

solution.exhibit_text:
Category: Inference
Getting to the Answer: Broad questions about the author's view are difficult to predict. Keep the Main Idea and the tone of the passage in mind. Evaluate each choice by comparing it strictly to the passage. Eliminate (A) as Out of Scope. The passage never connects COBOL's success to resistance to the first compiler. Eliminate (B) as Opposite. Paragraph 13 indicates that writing code in Python and Java uses Hopper's concepts, which included FLOW-MATIC philosophy. The languages are thus part of the same lineage, not fundamentally different. (C) is correct. Throughout the passage, the author emphasizes the "human side of computing" (paragraph 1), the "prejudice" of mathematicians (paragraph 6), and computing being for "everyone" (paragraph 13). This choice captures the author's primary argument: that Hopper transformed access to computing. She broke down the math-only barrier, making technology "accessible to people who weren't mathematicians" (paragraph 1). (D) is Out of Scope. The passage never implies modern programmers are "less capable" than past programmers.

questions.question: Which sentence from the excerpt provides evidence that Hopper prioritized practical application over scientific debate?

options.A: "Hopper believed that a computer could be programmed to translate human words into computer commands." (paragraph 6)
options.B: "In 1952, she developed the A-0 System, the first compiler." (paragraph 6)
options.C: "Hopper realized she couldn't win the argument with theory; she had to win it with utility." (paragraph 7)
options.D: "She shifted her focus from scientific computing to business computing." (paragraph 7)

solution.exhibit_text:
Category: Detail
Getting to the Answer: Read the question carefully and put what you're looking for into your own words. You need evidence that Hopper was more interested in usefulness than in discussions. Now work through the choices. Eliminate (A). This choice describes a belief of Hopper that would make computers more practical, but it does not contrast this practicality with "scientific debate." Eliminate (B). This detail alone does not compare usefulness with theories and debate. (C) is correct. This sentence clearly states that Hopper didn't try to convince her critics with words ("debate"), but rather showed them that her invention was useful ("practical application"). (D) is incorrect because, although business computing is a practical application, this specific sentence only mentions the "shift" without explaining the underlying reason for her change in focus.

options.B: comparing the length of FLOW-MATIC programs to Python programs.
options.C: indicating how much clearer FLOW-MATIC programming is compared to programming that uses English words.

paragraphs.text: Today, airships are seen mostly as advertisements hovering in the sky over sporting events. Such companies as Goodyear®, Metropolitan Life®, and Fuji Film® have all made use of "blimps" in this way to the delight of spectators. But there was a time, before World War II, that blimps—as well as other lighter-than-air vehicles—were not just a charming diversion but actually used as a mode of transportation. One in particular, the German ship Hindenburg, was an incredible example of a commercial passenger aircraft capable of crossing the Atlantic Ocean. Tragically, on one fateful day, the path of airships was changed forever when, in spectacular fashion, the Hindenburg revealed the downside of the use of airships as transportation.

Airships enjoyed many advantages in the early twentieth century, and the Hindenburg was considered a one-of-a-kind example. When the 804-foot Hindenburg was launched in 1936, it was the largest airship in the world. Like most airships of the period, the Hindenburg was built with a solid frame that encased a simple balloon filled with a light gas—in this case, hydrogen. The Hindenburg was a product of some of the newest technology of its time with a frame constructed of an early aluminum alloy called duralumin, while its gas cells were reinforced with a new material known as latex. In an age when airplanes could not carry more than 10 passengers at a time, the Hindenburg could hold an astounding 1,002 passengers, twice as many as a modern jetliner. Thus, in many ways, it was an incredible specimen of modern advancements.

Despite these advantages, however, the Hindenburg was hampered by many of the same drawbacks that plagued other airships. Tickets to fly in the Hindenburg were not affordable for most people, so the customer base was extremely limited. This was due in part to the massive amount of fuel needed not only to fill the balloon but also to power its propellers, making this airship very expensive to operate. Even with all of that fuel, the Hindenburg flew at a mere 78 miles per hour—a snail's pace considering that it was used for transatlantic passenger service. Because any airship is essentially a balloon with an engine, it is extremely vulnerable to air currents and stormy weather, and the Hindenburg, despite its massive size, was no different.

The Hindenburg's fate, however, rested on its most dangerous characteristic and one it shared with other airships: the use of highly flammable hydrogen gas. Any spark or flame that came near the gas could cause a horrific explosion, which is exactly what happened. On May 6, 1937, as the Hindenburg was landing in Lakehurst, New Jersey, it suddenly burst into flames, killing 36 of the 97 passengers on board. This explosion destroyed the ship quickly; in a matter of just 34 seconds, the entire ship was engulfed in flames. Although the exact cause is still unknown, it is believed to have been caused by a discharge of static electricity in the air that reacted to gas that had escaped from a small leak in the balloon. Though there had been other airship mishaps before this date, something about this particular disaster captured the public imagination—maybe the fact that it was famously witnessed and reported live by radio reporter Herbert Morrison, who gave a dramatic account of the event as it unfolded, or maybe it was just a final symbolic end to a mode of travel that had become passé.

At the time of the Hindenburg disaster, the airship was already obsolete as a mode of transportation. By the 1940s, commercial airplanes had advanced in development far beyond the airship's capacity. Now, modern airplanes cost much less to operate and fly at more than seven times the speed of the Hindenburg. Meanwhile, airline tickets are also far more affordable than airship travel ever was. The airship thus sank into permanently outdated status as a passenger service and acquired its modern-day role as a quirky advertising platform.

paragraphs.text: Many novice gardeners believe that once they find the "perfect spot" for their tomatoes or peppers, they should return to that same patch of earth year after year. However, successful long-term gardening relies on a practice known as crop rotation. This systematic approach involves changing the location of specific plant families each season to maintain soil health and disrupt the life cycles of pests.

To understand why rotation is necessary, one must look beneath the surface at the chemical composition of the soil. Different plants have varying "appetites" for primary macronutrients: nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K). Leafy greens, such as spinach and kale, are heavy nitrogen feeders, using the element to fuel rapid vegetative growth. Conversely, fruiting plants such as tomatoes require more phosphorus for bloom production and potassium for overall disease resistance and water regulation. If a gardener plants nitrogen-hungry kale in the same spot three years in a row, the soil becomes depleted of its nitrogen, leading to stunted, yellowing crops regardless of how much water they receive.

Beyond preventing nutrient depletion, crop rotation serves as a natural form of pest control. Many soil-borne pathogens and insect larvae are host-specific. For example, the spores of Phytophthora infestans (late blight) can linger in the soil where potatoes or tomatoes were grown. By moving these plants, which belong to the "nightshade" family of crops, to a different bed the following year and replacing them with a different family, such as legumes (beans and peas), the gardener effectively starves the remaining pathogens.

Furthermore, legumes offer a unique chemical advantage: they are "nitrogen fixers." Through a symbiotic relationship with Rhizobium bacteria in their root nodules, they convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form that stays in the ground. When these plants die and decompose, they leave behind a store of nitrogen for the next heavy-feeding crop. By understanding these subterranean chemical exchanges, a backyard gardener transforms from a mere planter into a steward of a complex, living ecosystem.

ela_passages.intro_note: Marek, the narrator, is completing his last day of volunteering at the local animal shelter for a high school volunteer project.

paragraphs.text: Charlie, a chocolate lab mix with oversized paws and a lolling tongue, is one of my favorites at the Animal Shelter. She's been here since a kind-hearted soul brought her and her four siblings in after the mother had been found in an alley. A rescuer had taken the litter and mother until they could eat on their own, then returned the puppies for adoption. One by one, her siblings found homes, but Charlie's energetic behavior seemed to deter even the most fearless of children and patient of adopters. In the eight months that I had been walking the dogs at the shelter, only Charlie still pulled ahead or turned the leash into a chew toy.

The volunteer coordinator, Ireland, smiled as I returned. Charlie appeared to have gained energy from the walk rather than expending any. When Ireland directed another volunteer to take Charlie for another walk, the volunteer sighed audibly before dragging his feet and Charlie back out to the field. I watched the enthusiastic puppy and the decidedly unenthusiastic walker. I wondered how many other volunteers just tolerated Charlie, who was easily the best dog in the place.
"We're all going to miss you, but I think Charlie is gonna miss you most of all," Ireland said, seeing my focus on the retreating figures.
"I wish I could stay, but I need to start working. I'm gonna need a car for college, and my parents can't afford it," I responded, turning back to Ireland.
"And I wish we could afford to pay you to walk her, but that's the downside of being a non-profit," Ireland responded.

"I know. That's why we only get paid with dog kisses and cat scratches," I said, shrugging off a little sadness that I couldn't afford to just adopt Charlie. But getting a dog only a year before leaving for college wasn't a good idea.
She smiled at me kindly, as if she could hear my thoughts, and turned back to organizing a box of newly donated chew toys.

I left the storage area, intending to head to the kitten corner before clocking out for the day, when I passed a family walking through the outdoor kennels. I overheard the child exclaim about the rather distinct smell of so many animals in one space. It reminded me of when I first started volunteering to complete the community service hours required by my high school. I was not happy that my only option—due to my schedule and reliance on the bus route—was volunteering at my local animal shelter. A few of my friends, with their own cars or more flexible schedules, had scored gigs at offices or for local events. Both were probably a lot cleaner and cooler than this would be.

After my mom had dropped me off at the shelter, I signed in and proceeded to the small multipurpose room. There were about a dozen others with varying degrees of interest in being there. I sat at the back, prepared to listen to a boring speech about unwanted animals, sad surrender stories, and a task list we'd be expected to do every day. Instead, Ireland, a short, gray-haired woman with the energy of a border collie, opened with a video of the funny antics the shelter had caught on tape. She shared heartwarming stories of successful adoptions, statistics about their rescues, and the most optimistic view of the future.

"The job may stink—because all animals poop—and, yes, there's some tragedy in this line of work. But you'll learn more about humanity, and your own connection to it, working here than you will anywhere else. And if dog kisses and cat scratches were dimes, you'd be a millionaire by August," Ireland said, concluding her presentation.
She took us on a tour of the shelter. The good feelings made by the presentation were quickly wiped away by the stench of the outdoor kennels.
"Ugh! Why does it smell like this?" A young girl exclaimed, covering her nose and mouth with the collar of her shirt.
"Scared and lonely dogs who have undiagnosed nutritional needs," Ireland said, losing a bit of the humor she had been showing.
"Why do you treat them like this?" the girl asked.

"We don't treat them like this. Most of these dogs have been abandoned or anonymously surrendered, so we can't ask if they have certain food needs. They're scared because it's new, it's loud, and their family isn't here anymore, and they don't understand," Ireland answered.

That made me feel worse than the smell did. A crash against the chain link fence and a loud bark made a few of us jump. It was a large, dark brown puppy, whose feet seemed to be growing faster than the rest of her. She jumped against the fence again, seeming to say, "Hi Friends! Play? Run? Play?" If dogs could smile optimistically, that's exactly what you'd say she was doing.
"Charlie!" an old volunteer called, "Down!"

Charlie dropped paws to the ground with her tail wagging like an engine revving, which caused her whole body to vibrate. Her two kennel mates, also brown dogs, lay quietly on the concrete, clearly unable to keep up with Charlie.
I had to laugh because Charlie reminded me so much of my little sister Andra, who always had time for fun. Crouching down, I scratched her ears through the fence.
"Some won't ever understand why their siblings keep leaving, but they stay here." Ireland continued, unaffected by Charlie's exuberance.
We continued on, following Ireland through the many different and essential areas of the shelter.

Looking back now, I realize how much this experience has changed my life. I never knew how much I'd enjoy getting to know the animals and people here or that it'd lead me to the perfect job—dogwalking in my neighborhood. The experience gave me so much more than I had anticipated, and I worried I would never be able to return the favor.
I worried that I would also be one more person to leave Charlie behind. Would she miss me as much as I would miss her?
I said goodbye to the staff and other volunteers on my way out and headed to my bus stop. The walk was harder than I expected, but I hoped that it was one I would be able to walk again.
